title: The mongoose and the five daily offerings
word: with the Keeper's framing of what
hookLine: a half-gold mongoose at a king's great sacrifice, and the handful of rice some homes still set out
carry: a home's five daily offerings: pancha mahayajna
tomorrow: what did one man do with the book, instead of arguing with it?

cards: King Yudhishthira has just finished a great horse sacrifice, gifts piled high. Then a mongoose walks in, half its body gold, and says: this sacrifice isn't worth one poor family's barley flour. Everyone stares.
The mongoose explains. In a famine, a poor family who lived by gleaning had one small portion of barley left. A hungry guest came to the door.

The father gave his share. Then the mother, then the son, then the son's wife, until the guest was fed and they had nothing. The mongoose rolled where that flour had fallen, and half of him turned gold.
He's been rolling at great sacrifices ever since, looking for the other half.

teach.b: The tradition has a name for what that family did. The Manusmriti's third chapter gives every householder five great offerings, the pancha mahayajna, to keep each day.

In paraphrase: study is the offering to the Veda; water and food for the ancestors, the offering to them; the offering into the fire, to the gods; food set out for creatures, the bali, to all beings; and honoring guests, to people.
So a yajna isn't only a grand fire rite with priests.
The book even says why it's daily: a home harms small lives without meaning to, at the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and the water pot, and these offerings answer that harm.
Many readers hear the mongoose the same way: the family's barley outweighed the king's gold because it was everything they had, given to a guest.

That's why some Hindu homes still set a little rice out for the crows before eating, and feed a guest first. In a city flat, it can be the first plate for whoever drops by. And it's the other side of this stretch.

teach.h: EVERY HOME FEEDS CREATURES AND GUESTS.
teach.b: The same book that ranked people by birth asked every home to feed creatures and strangers each day. Some keep the rice without keeping the rest.

how: Some Hindu households set aside a little food each day for birds, cows or other creatures before eating, and some keep the custom of feeding a guest as an honored visitor.

games.q: what does “with the keeper's framing of what” mean?
o: what a tradition keeps, even from a book it doesn't
the five rooms of a traditional Hindu house
the gifts a bride's family brings to a wedding

games.q: the daily five — tap the pairs.
p: a family's barley outweighed a king's gifts

s: a yajna is always a big fire ritual run by priests
Manu's daily five include study, ancestors, creatures and guests; and in the Mahabharata a family's barley for a guest outweighs a king's sacrifice.
the Manusmriti names small harms a home does without meaning to
the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and the water pot.

games.q: your grandmother keeps one daily rite that comes from a book you've learned to criticize. what fits this stretch's idea?
o: keeping a part isn't keeping the whole; ask what she keeps, and why.
read her the book's worst lines so she'll stop.
assume she agrees with every line in it.
games.why: keeping and rejecting runs right through books: some homes keep the handful of rice without keeping the rest.

practice: If there's any food near you, a few grains of rice, a piece of fruit, a cracker, hold it and smell it slowly. Break off a small part and set it aside, for a bird, or for whoever comes.
Then taste the rest, and let the taste stay on your tongue until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Kept and rejected, inside one book: the pancha mahayajna, five daily offerings that some homes keep from a book they don't keep whole.

orig.note: Sanskrit pancha mahayajna, the householder's five great offerings.

carryVoice: Keep this one: a home's five daily offerings, the pancha mahayajna. A half-gold mongoose knows what they're worth. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Manusmriti 3.67–3.74 (the five great sacrifices: study, ancestors, fire, creatures, guests, 3.70)
Manusmriti 3.68 (the householder's hearth, grinding stone, broom, mortar and pestle, and water pot)
Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva (the half-golden mongoose at Yudhishthira's horse sacrifice; the gleaner's family who gave their barley flour to a guest)
